newsitem.title: USA: Clinton surgery goes without a hitch - White House.
newsitem.headline: Clinton surgery goes without a hitch - White House.

text.p: President Bill Clinton came through emergency knee surgery successfully and without complications on Friday, serenaded by country music recordings and determined to keep a U.S.-Russia summit date next week, the White House said.

"No complications were reported to me," White House spokesman Mike McCurry said at Bethesda Naval Hospital as orthopedic surgeons finished up on work that reattached a right-knee tendon Clinton tore when he stumbled on a stair early Friday.
"They were very pleased with the surgery and with the outcome," McCurry said.

Clinton, 50, was expected to be wheeled to his hospital room, where wife Hillary and daughter Chelsea awaited him, for a stay of at least one night. Doctors said he would then be equipped with a knee brace and crutches for some weeks.

"He was very talkative and cheerful during the procedure" and alert most of the time, although he apparently dozed off now and then, McCurry said. At one point he asked for a book to pass the time but the doctors turned him down.
He chose tapes by country singers Lyle Lovett and Jimmy Buffett to accompany the surgery over an operating room speaker system, the White House said.

Clinton had a "regional" anaesthetic that numbed him approximately from the mid-section down, so that he was never rendered unconscious, the spokesman said. Constitutional procedures for shifting authority temporarily to Vice President Al Gore were therefore not necessary.
Surgery began at 2:39 p.m. EST (1939 GMT), McCurry said, and lasted over two hours.
Clinton caught his heel on a step at the Florida estate of Australian golfer Greg Norman early on Friday, tearing the quadriceps tendon connecting the kneecap to the upper thigh in his right leg.

The knee-buckling tumble -- "he heard a very loud pop," one aide said -- will put Clinton on crutches for weeks, but he insisted it would not delay his summit with Russian President Boris Yeltsin in Helsinki, Finland, next week.
"The president informed the doctors that he will be going to Helsinki on Tuesday and they said, 'yes sir,' they understood that," McCurry said.
Hillary Rodham Clinton planned to go ahead with a two-week tour of six African nations, but was delaying her departure by one day, until Sunday, to see her husband through the start of his recovery.

McCurry said the incident was also one factor in the postponement of the planned White House visit of Jordan's King Hussein scheduled for Tuesday. Hussein's visit had been in doubt anyway due to the faltering pace of the Middle East peace process.
Doctors had to drill holes in the kneecap and in the tendon and run sutures through the holes to reattach the tendon, which controls the ability to straighten the leg.
"This is not a terribly severe injury and not a terribly complicated operation to perform," Dr. David Wade, chief of the naval hospital's clinical staff, said as surgery began.
Instead of a cast, his knee will be placed in a brace to give him some mobility but to protect the leg, Wade said.
McCurry said Clinton asked typical patient's questions such as how long it would be before he could run or swing a golf club again.

Wade said Clinton would remain at least overnight at the hospital and possibly until Sunday, then faced four to five months of rehabilitation before he can hit golf balls again, and perhaps six months before he can jog.

A senior State Department official said another possible diplomatic casualty of the presidential mishap could be a scheduled Monday meeting with Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov, which might have to be scrapped. Primakov arrives in Washington over the weekend for talks to prepare the Helsinki summit.
